title: Show HN: A layer on top llama.cpp enabling big MoE streaming on phone and laptop
content:
Big local AI agents, on every edge device.
  An adaptive streaming optimizer for Mixture-of-Experts models.
Any hardware, any OS, any model, any quantization, behind a local OpenAI-compatible server.
  ▶ Watch the full two-minute demo
Real recordings on a 16 GB laptop and a 12 GB Android phone. Sped-up parts are marked.
A Mixture-of-Experts model uses only a few of its experts for each token. BigMoeOnEdge keeps in memory what every token needs and streams the rest from storage, exactly when it is needed. A model several times larger than RAM runs, and its output is identical to running it fully in memory.
- Adaptive streaming optimizer. The planner measures the machine (memory, storage speed, every CPU, GPU and NPU) and builds the plan for that exact device: what stays in memory, what streams, which chip reads the prompt and which writes the answer. It shows the reason behind every choice. No flags, no tuning.
- Any hardware, any OS. Android, macOS, Windows and Linux ship today, with iOS on the way. CPU, GPU and NPU backends load as modules, and the planner uses whichever the machine has.
- Any model, any quantization. Any MoE gguf that llama.cpp loads. Search Hugging Face from the app, and the engine reads the model's header before the download and tells you how it will run.
- A local OpenAI-compatible server. Every device serves the models it runs, so chat clients and coding agents such as opencode work fully local. A phone can serve a laptop over Wi-Fi.
Real runs, measured live. They are examples, not limits: the engine fits itself to whatever it runs on, and stronger hardware runs faster.
Every figure, the configuration behind it and the method: docs/benchmarks.md.
Got a machine that is not here? Run scripts/bench-report.sh /path/to/model.gguf and paste the
table into a benchmark report.
Phone (Android). Install the APK from the latest release, pick a model under Models, and chat. Settings → Serve on the network shares it with other devices, with a key.
Desktop (macOS, Windows, Linux). Download the bmoe-desktop archive from the same release and
run bmoe-server --open. The app opens at http://127.0.0.1:8765/.
Command line.
bmoe-cli -m model.gguf --auto -p "Explain MoE routing."   # measure, plan, run
bmoe-cli -m model.gguf --plan                              # show the plan and exit
The phone and the desktop show the same five screens: Chat, Models, Plan, Settings and Metrics.
Any OpenAI client works with the local address:
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8765/v1", api_key="local")
reply = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="local",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a haiku about experts on flash."}],
)
print(reply.choices[0].message.content)
Streaming, tool calls and reasoning are supported. For opencode, add the server as an
OpenAI-compatible provider with baseURL set to http://127.0.0.1:8765/v1. To serve other machines,
start the server with --host and --api-key. The full API: docs/server-api.md.
The engine is built on llama.cpp's public API, so every quantization, tokenizer and chat template llama.cpp supports works unchanged, and a new llama.cpp release is a submodule bump. Which tensors are the routed experts is read from the file itself, so new MoE architectures need no code here (docs/which-models-stream.md).
Correctness is a test, not a promise: ctest checks that streaming gives output identical to
running with every expert in memory, across the cache, evictions, overlap, sessions and split
models. docs/architecture.md.
The planner reads the model's shape from its header and measures the machine it runs on. Its rules name no platform and no device, so a phone and a laptop get different plans from the same rules. A setting you pass by hand is never overruled. The Plan screen shows the result: a one-line summary, where the memory goes, what each device does, and every decision with its reason. docs/hardware-planning.md.
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on a 12 GB Android phone, real time: the answer, then the plan it runs.
Backends load as modules beside the engine, so a CUDA, HIP or SYCL module built with its own toolchain loads like the shipped ones. Details, and what was measured where: docs/platforms.md.
git clone --recursive https://github.com/Helldez/BigMoeOnEdge.git
cd BigMoeOnEdge
cd ui && npm ci && npm run build && cd ..
scripts/build-host.sh
build/bin/bmoe-server --open
Tests: cd build && ctest --output-on-failure (needs python3 with the gguf package). Android:
scripts/build-android.ps1, then the APK in examples/android.
CONTRIBUTING.md.
docs/, indexed by what you are trying to do. Start with hardware-planning.md, settings.md, server-api.md, platforms.md and limitations.md.
Ideas from AirLLM, Apple's LLM in a flash, FlexGen, PowerInfer and EdgeMoE, packaged on top of llama.cpp. The closest recent work is flash-moe, a Metal engine that streams a 397B MoE from SSD on Apple Silicon; BigMoeOnEdge takes llama.cpp's public API across architectures and platforms instead.
Apache-2.0. See LICENSE.

report.summary: BigMoeOnEdge adds an adaptive streaming layer on top of llama.cpp so phones and laptops can run Mixture-of-Experts models several times larger than their RAM with bit-identical output.
report.background: Mixture-of-Experts models activate only a handful of experts per token, so a 35B-parameter model may compute with ~3B active parameters. That makes them cheap to run in FLOPs but not in memory: every expert's weights still have to live somewhere. On a phone or a 16 GB laptop, the model often exceeds RAM by several times. A body of research — Apple's 'LLM in a flash', FlexGen, PowerInfer, EdgeMoE, AirLLM — attacked this by keeping hot weights in memory and streaming cold ones from flash storage. More recently flash-moe did it for a 397B MoE on Apple Silicon via Metal. BigMoeOnEdge packages the same idea as a general layer over llama.cpp's public API, so any MoE GGUF, quantization and platform llama.cpp supports inherits streaming without a custom engine, aimed squarely at the current wave of local agents and on-device chat.
key_points: An adaptive planner measures the machine — RAM, storage speed, CPU, GPU and NPU — then decides what stays resident, what streams, and which chip handles prompt processing versus token generation. It exposes the reasoning behind every decision in a Plan screen. No flags or manual tuning are required, and any setting passed by hand is never overruled.

At runtime the engine keeps the experts each token actually needs in memory and streams the rest from storage exactly when required. The project treats correctness as a test rather than a claim: ctest verifies streaming output is identical to running every expert fully in memory, covering cache behavior, evictions, overlap, sessions and split model files.

It runs on Android, macOS, Windows and Linux (iOS promised), with CPU, GPU and NPU backends loaded as separate modules so CUDA, HIP or SYCL builds drop in with their own toolchain. Every device exposes an OpenAI-compatible server, so chat clients and coding agents like opencode run fully local, and a phone can serve a laptop over Wi-Fi with an API key.

Because it builds on llama.cpp's public API, any MoE GGUF and quantization works unchanged, and new llama.cpp releases are a submodule bump. The engine reads the model header to identify which tensors are routed experts, so new MoE architectures need no new code — and it can predict how a model will run before you download it.

The README shows real, measured runs — Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on a 12 GB Android phone and a 16 GB laptop — with configurations and methodology published in docs/benchmarks.md. A bench-report script lets anyone reproduce and submit numbers for hardware not yet covered, which is the honest way to build credibility for streaming claims.
report.impact: This matters because the binding constraint on local AI has shifted from compute to memory capacity and bandwidth. If streaming MoE works as advertised across commodity hardware, the practical ceiling for on-device models rises from 'what fits in RAM' to 'what fits on disk' — a 5–10x jump for phones and consumer laptops. For developers, an OpenAI-compatible local endpoint means existing agent frameworks, IDE assistants and evaluation harnesses work with no rewrites, and the planner's transparency makes performance predictable rather than a tuning exercise. For regular users, it points toward private, offline assistants running models that would today require a workstation. The caveats are real: SSD latency and endurance, thermal throttling on phones, and token rates that will be far below datacenter speeds.
report.tools: Start with llama.cpp itself, since BigMoeOnEdge is a layer over its public API. Pair it with Hugging Face GGUF MoE releases (Qwen3-MoE, gpt-oss, DeepSeek variants) and a client such as opencode or any OpenAI SDK. For context, read the prior art the authors cite: AirLLM, PowerInfer, FlexGen, EdgeMoE, Apple's 'LLM in a flash' paper, and flash-moe for the Metal/Apple Silicon comparison. Run scripts/bench-report.sh on your own hardware to see whether streaming beats simply using a smaller model.
